items.text: **A third of the API surface is a provisional draft named after a screen title, and the count is exact.** Measured 8 September: **577 of the package's 1,626 operations carry `x-ticvai-provisional: true`, and for all 577 — every single one — the `summary` is verbatim the title of the screen in its own `x-ticvai-consumed-by`.** Not most of them; all of them. The operations state it themselves: *"Drafted from the workshop pack; the shape below is read out of it, not invented... Still provisional. A shape read out of a PDF has not been agreed with anyone who has to build it, and the schema says so in its own persistence tag: it is a request, not a table."* **This is the same defect as the 423 title-stamped screens, one layer down**, and the two corroborate each other in the way that proves nothing: `check-screens` verifies that every screen's operations resolve to a contract, and 577 of those contracts were written from the screens. **Two derived artefacts agreeing is not corroboration** — Claude Design's own caution about the layout check, arriving from the contract side. **It is why CF-170's Class B cannot be fixed by adding operations** and why any count of *contracted* coverage is 35% softer than it reads. **Audited against the source packs 8 September, and the 577 are sound.** Every provisional description cites its origin as `<pack>, page N`. Checked against the 39 client Design Books in `OneDrive_1_8-9-2026.zip`: **577 of 577 citations resolve to a real pack, and not one cites a page beyond that pack's length** — 573 distinct pages across 17 books, maximum cited page inside the book's page count in every case. **They are not invented and they are not unverifiable.** The `provisional` flag means *not yet agreed with whoever builds it*, which is an honest label rather than a defect, and the summaries matching screen titles is what you get when a screen and an operation are read out of the same page of the same pack. **The real gap is the other direction, and it is larger: 22 of the 39 Design Books have no operation drafted from them at all** — 1,323 pages of client design material against 1,058 pages that were used. The biggest untouched are Retail (202pp), Inventory & Procurement (175pp), Resource Management (169pp), F&B Backend (130pp), Wallet (129pp) and Finance (123pp) — **which is CF-164 and CF-125 seen from the source side**: the F&B/Retail/Procurement/Inventory workshop that is outstanding in three consecutive MoMs is exactly the material nobody has drafted from. **Recommendation: stop treating the 577 as the problem.** Schedule the workshops to agree them, and open the 22 uncited books as the scoping question they actually are

items.text: **Seventeen screens promise a publication their declared operations cannot perform, and five of them are a broken workflow rather than a naming defect.** Found by Claude Design 8 September, extending the rule package-wide from the nine already recorded. **Class B is the one to raise first: five screens can approve and cannot publish** — `BO-293` Membership Product Validation, `BO-353` Multi-Media Preview, `ADM-247` Versioning & Governance, `CMS-030` Privacy Configuration Testing and `CMS-050` Waiver Approval each declare only an `approve*` operation against a title ending in *Publication*. **An approval with nothing to release is a dead end in the workflow**, not a name to tidy: somebody signs off and the thing they signed off cannot go live. **Class A is eleven title-only screens** declaring a single `list*` — `BO-173`, `BO-193`, `BO-203`, `BO-213`, `BO-223`, `BO-233`, `ADM-085`, `ADM-143`, `ADM-227`, `ADM-307`, `CMS-033` — which is re-signature work and is why the six of them in the 8 September patch were correctly held rather than given `publishGate`. **Class C is one screen that monitors what it creates**: `ADM-115 Live Dynamic Price Execution & Deployment Monitor` declares `createLiveDynamicPrice`. **Class D is one false positive to exclude**: `ADM-029 Deployment Monitor` declares `startRollout`, `pauseRollout` and `rollbackRollout` and is a real deployment actor — the rule caught it because rollout control is not named `publish*`. **Each class needs a different remedy**, which is the reason for classing them: B needs operations added to contracts, A needs titles or operations decided, C needs one of the two names changed, D needs nothing. **Recommendation: take Class B first** — it is five contract additions against a workflow that currently cannot complete **Checked 8 September, and Class B is not five contract additions. Do not add the operations.** All five `approve*` operations carry `x-ticvai-provisional: true` and `tags: [drafted]`, and **every one of their summaries is verbatim the title of the screen that consumes it** — `approveMembershipProductValidation` summarises as *Membership Product Validation, Approval, Publication & Versioning*. Their own descriptions say so: *"drafted from the workshop pack... a shape read out of a PDF has not been agreed with anyone who has to build it."* **So the approval step does not exist either** — the operation naming it is a provisional draft named after the screen, which is Class A's defect one layer down in the contracts. Adding five `publish*` siblings would invent agreed API surface on top of unagreed drafts. **The remedy is to de-provisionalise the five with someone who has to build them**, and the publication either falls out of that conversation or the titles were wrong. See CF-171 for the population this belongs to **Narrowed 20 September from seventeen screens to sixteen, by re-testing all of them against the current screen definitions.** **Class D is confirmed a false positive and is withdrawn**: `ADM-029 Deployment Monitor` declares twelve operations including `startRollout`, `pauseRollout` and `rollbackRollout`, and is a real deployment actor the rule caught only because rollout control is not named `publish*`. **Class B is confirmed still broken** — `BO-293`, `BO-353`, `ADM-247`, `CMS-030` and `CMS-050` each still declare exactly one operation and it is an `approve*`, so somebody signs off and the thing they signed off cannot go live. Five need contract work; the eleven of Class A need a title-or-operation decision, not an operation each.

items.text: **Three places where the data model was built and no screen was ever written, and one where the reverse is true.** ADR-0041 turns 57 command centres into rows in `reporting.dashboard`, which needs **three or four authoring screens that do not exist**: a dashboard list separating mine from shared, an editor that adds a tile and binds it to a `report_definition`, a tile configuration panel for `visualisation`, `parameters` and `refresh_seconds`, and a viewer if the editor is not also one. Searching all 1,091 screen names for `widget`, `saved view`, `drag`, `layout editor` or `add a tile` returns **nothing**, while the tables, the four operations and a `tiles` array capped at 24 all exist. **Two further decisions ride on it**: the editor must surface `dashboard.aggregate_cost` and `report_definition.estimated_cost`, because 24 tiles on a short refresh is a performance incident nobody was warned about; and there is no `deleteDashboard` — `list`, `create`, `get`, `update` and nothing else — so a soft or hard delete has to be chosen where `is_shared` is true. **The same shape appears twice more, from the other side**: `seatp` has 13 boards and 130 screens of seat-map authoring with no package counterpart at all — no `canvas`, `section`, `suite` or `seating chart` screen exists against a `seating` schema of 14 tables — and `crm` has a Guest Directory, Activity Timeline and Corporate & Groups the package never specified. **Design that exists and specs that do not, next to specs that exist and screens that do not.** Recommendation: take the four dashboard screens as the first tranche, since the contract and DDL are already there and it unblocks deleting 57

items.text: **Three deployment scenarios were requested and the package models one.** The 24 August session asks Softlabs to document (a) independent tenant deployment, (b) centralized/shared platform for small-to-medium tenants, (c) **dedicated infrastructure for large/mega events and flash sales** — each with an architecture diagram, auto-scaling behaviour and failure handling. **ADR-0001 models one cell per jurisdiction and nothing else.** (a) and (b) are variations on it; **(c) is new and nothing in the package describes it** — a short-lived environment standing up for one sale, taking tens of thousands of concurrent users within hours, then going away. **That is not a cell.** It has no tenancy of its own, it reads a catalogue it does not own, and its orders have to land in the permanent platform afterwards. **The reconciliation path back is the part with no design**, and it is the same shape as the offline sync problem one layer up. **Narrowed 20 September to the reconciliation path, which still has no design.** The environment's shape is settled by [ADR-0047](../adr/0047-how-long-data-is-kept-and-where-it-goes-next.md): a burst environment is a pinned `control.cell_instance` with `role: burst`, no `cell_tenant` of its own and a read-only catalogue replica. **It is never placed onto and never enters another instance's placement metric** — a flash sale that joined the trailing average would poison a region's placement for a week after it ended. Its data retention is `reconciled + 30 days` rather than a lifetime, so it is auditable like every other retention in the package.

To illustrate the scale difference, Qossai gave two contrasting examples: a stadium such as Real Madrid's (~60,000 seats) could sell out within a few hours of tickets going live for a major event, generating extremely high concurrent load, whereas a client like a water park or museum might see a maximum of around 2,000 visitors per day — a much lower and steadier load (roughly five people per minute). The system therefore needs a plan that can fit both extremes without over- or under-provisioning either type of client, which points to an auto-scaling architecture rather than a fixed one. items.text: **Consent, retention and archival were walked in the 20 August CRM session and the package has consent only.** `recordConsent` exists, CF-160 settled that a merge takes the narrower of two consents, and `pii` is separate from `identity` so a subject-access export is answerable. **Retention and archival are not modelled anywhere.** The session covered *"consent policy, data privacy and retention/archival"* as one topic; the package treats the first two as solved and **has no operation, no column and no policy for how long a guest profile is kept or what happens to it afterwards.** CF-64 counts 89 retention requirements against two stated periods — **this is the same hole seen from the CRM side rather than the infrastructure side**, and the two registers have not been read against each other. **Decided 20 September by [ADR-0047](../adr/0047-how-long-data-is-kept-and-where-it-goes-next.md) and not yet built**, which is why it stays open — the rule CF-135 set is decided *and* built. The archive is a separate instance rather than a tablespace, so archived personal data is not one query mistake from an operational read. **Derived stores purge at archive, not at erasure**: a knowledge base still answering from an archived profile is an archive that did not happen, and nothing cascades between Postgres and Qdrant. Five contract changes are named and ordered; `pii.subject` already carries `is_erased`, `erased_at` and `erasure_request_id`, so erasure is already a tombstone — **but no erase operation exists**, and `ai.yaml` names `pii.erase_subject` as the erasure path.

items.text: **The delivery plan prices 7,552 person-days and its priorities contradict the dependency order the walk found.** `sources/planning/TAIS_Product_Planning_and_Delivery_Plan_4_1.xlsx` had never entered the package either — 23 epics, 445 features, 2,173 tasks, a milestone plan, a dependency matrix and a Jira import, covering 3,332 requirements. **It is a good document and two things in it need reconciling.** **(1) Resource Management is P3 — Could, at 63 matrix requirements**, and it is the single most-depended-on gap in the walk: CF-125 is cited by rows in five domains, and rentals, lockers, cabanas, instructor assignment, event resourcing, maintenance resource planning and 7.6's fifteen-row rental module all sit behind it. **A P3 prerequisite blocks every P1 that needs it.** **Access Control System is also P3 at 114 requirements**, which reads as a scoring artefact rather than a judgement — `access` is one of the best-covered contracts in the package and gate entry is the operational core. **(2) The plan splits one module across three priorities** — Notifications and Messaging appears at P1, P2 and P3; Loyalty at P1, P2 and P3; Portfolio at P1, P2 and P3; Digital Waivers at P1 and P2 — so a module is partly must-have and partly could-have, which is not a schedulable statement. **The plan's own *Missing Components* sheet independently reaches several of the walk's conclusions** — ABAC policy engine (CF-130), central monitoring and alerting (CF-134), a single notification service (BL-052), developer portal and OpenAPI docs (CF-135), performance budget (BL-098) — and marks **DevOps/IaC and CI/CD as outright MISSING**, which matches the package holding no SQL, no code and no Sprint 0. **Recommendation: re-derive priority from the dependency matrix rather than from requirement counts**, and reconcile against the 178 backlog entries before the plan is used to schedule anything **Deferred to the reconciliation — Chinmay, 18 August.** Finished once the milestone-to-wave reconciliation is done. **Resource Management's P3 rating is already resolved**: CF-125 puts it in scope, which was half of this conflict.

items.text: **The platform cannot issue a tax invoice, and in the UAE that is a VAT obligation rather than a document feature.** 5.7.93 requires tax invoices, simplified invoices, corporate invoices and consolidated invoices; 5.7.94 requires full and partial credit memos linked to them; 5.10.3 requires the receipt to show *"all required fields in accordance with VAT regulations"* and **nothing anywhere states what those fields are.** `finance` is otherwise strong here — `LegalEntity` carries `taxRegistrationNumber`, `countryCode`, `currencyScale` and `fiscalYearStartMonth`; `TaxCode` supports compound tax, inclusive and exclusive treatment and effective dating; the ledger is append-only with reversal rather than edit. **The data exists and the document does not.** `subscription.generateInvoice` bills a tenant for the platform, which is a different payer, a different ledger and a different format. **Three things make this a decision rather than a build item.** A UAE tax invoice has a **mandated format** — supplier TRN, sequential numbering that cannot gap, prescribed fields, Arabic where required — and issuing a non-compliant one is a finding at audit, not a formatting complaint. **A credit memo is the paired obligation**: a refund against a tax invoice is not simply a reversing journal, it is a document with its own sequence. And **sequential numbering interacts with ADR-0013 and ADR-0014** — a local-first till that journals offline and a cell-per-region topology both make a single gapless sequence harder than it looks, and the answer differs by whether numbering is per legal entity, per venue or per till. **Also unresolved: e-invoicing.** The UAE is phasing in mandatory e-invoicing, and whether that binds in the delivery window is a question for the client's finance function rather than for us **To Qossai and finance — Chinmay, 18 August.** The open question is what a UAE tax invoice must contain: **5.10.3 requires *all required fields in accordance with VAT regulations* and nothing states what those fields are.** `finance` already carries the TRN, compound tax and inclusive treatment; the gap is the document.

items.text: **Cookie consent management is fifteen requirements, a regulatory obligation, and normally bought rather than built.** 2.6.51–2.6.65 ask for a consent banner with configurable layouts and languages, cookie categorisation into strictly-necessary, functional, analytics and marketing, **automatic site scanning to detect new and third-party cookies, pixel tags and tracking technologies**, script blocking so analytics and advertising tags do not load before consent, a preference centre, consent records with timestamp and identifier, an audit trail of withdrawals, multi-domain preference sharing, consent analytics and an administration portal. **2.6.60 names GDPR, the ePrivacy Directive, CCPA, CPRA, LGPD and PDPL**, so this is compliance rather than preference. **The package has one trace: `PolicyKind.cookie`, a policy document a tenant can publish.** That is the text, not the enforcement. **`marketing-crm` does hold a real PDPL consent register** — purposes of marketing, personalisation, profiling, thirdPartySharing, aiProcessing and transactional, with `noticeVersion`, `expiresAfterMonths`, `isRequiredForService`, source per channel and full history — **and it answers a different question.** Consent to process a guest's data for marketing is not consent to set a tracking cookie on a browser, the legal bases differ, and the second has to be enforced client-side before a script loads. **The decision is build, buy or drop.** Cookie scanning means maintaining a cookie database and re-scanning as third-party tags change, which is the product OneTrust and Cookiebot sell; building it is a standing maintenance commitment on a platform whose scope is venue operations. Buying it means a vendor on every tenant storefront and a data-residency question under ADR-0009. **Dropping it is only available if no tenant storefront sets a non-essential cookie**, which the analytics requirements elsewhere in the matrix contradict **To Qossai — Chinmay, 18 August.** Cookie consent is a buy-or-build decision, not a design one, and **script blocking is the part that makes it a product rather than a form.** OneTrust and Cookiebot exist.

items.text: **Biometric data is sensitive under PDPL** — heightened protection, explicit consent, DPIA, stricter transfer rules. Affects Face Pass, facial readers and fingerprint enrolment. Not previously flagged; the current design treats biometrics as ordinary identity data. **A deviation was built on 21 September and is recorded here rather than discovered in UAT.** 3.2.44 describes Face Tag and states that it *"does not require the customer to explicitly sign a consent form"*. **BL-106 built it requiring explicit consent anyway.** **PDPL Article 4 admits no legitimate-interests basis** — its exceptions are an exhaustive list — so there is no lawful route to a consent-free biometric capture — a short life shortens what the consent is *for* and does not remove the need for it. **This is CF-130's shape**: a requirement asking for something the law does not allow, built the lawful way, with the difference written down. **What counsel needs to confirm is the form rather than the principle** — whether a notice acknowledged at a counter satisfies *explicit* for a same-visit tag, or whether a signature is required, because the first is operable at a gate and the second is not. `VenueSettings.biometrics` already makes the venue name a DPIA and acknowledge a consent notice before any of it can be switched on. **This conflict stays open on that one question** — the functionality is built and the principle is settled; what is outstanding is the form of consent counsel will accept at a gate.

Branded virtual waiting room: Activates automatically above a configurable concurrent-buyer threshold (example discussed: 500 concurrent buyers) during high-demand on-sales; shows a wait time and is branded consistently with the tenant's mobile app theme.

Key concern: virtual queue guests must not be merged into the same physical line as VIP guests, since VIP guests pay specifically to minimize their wait and enter within minutes of arriving — mixing the two would erode the VIP guest's paid value. A virtual queue guest, while not waiting in a physical line, has still effectively “waited” (e.g., 60 minutes) before their return window, so the operational model needs its own dedicated handling at the ride (e.g., a separate line, or scanning a QR code within a specific arrival window) distinct from both VIP and walk-in guests.

items.name: Parking Configuration
items.text: Answered by the 14 August MoM section 10, which this question was waiting for. Parking is barrier integration, in three models, and it is not space counting. (1) No integration - TICVAI issues its own QR and on-site security verifies it manually; (2) ANPR - the guest enters a plate at checkout and TICVAI pushes it to the parking system's whitelist so the barrier opens; (3) QR handoff - TICVAI sends a QR to the barrier for validation. Pay-per-hour parking is explicitly out of scope, handled by the parking vendor's own POS. So this is one configuration screen choosing a model and binding a vendor adaptor, not the three different screens the question feared - and ADR-0012's adaptor-first rule is what the minute asks for when it says a new parking vendor should take days rather than weeks. The `parking` module key in the White Label Builder now has something behind it.

hits.paragraph: Chinmay and Qossai reviewed three parking integration models: (1) no integration — TICVAI issues its own QR code and on-site security manually verifies it; (2) ANPR/plate-number integration — the guest enters their plate number at checkout, and TICVAI's API pushes the plate number to the parking system's whitelist so the barrier opens automatically; (3) QR-code handoff — TICVAI sends a QR code to the parking system's barrier for entry validation. A separate, pay-per-hour parking model (unrelated to ticketing) can be handled independently via the parking system's own POS. Qossai noted the team has integrated with such parking APIs before (consuming and pushing data) and that the architecture

Parking: Two supported models: (1) fully platform-native — guest purchases parking, receives a QR code scanned by a handheld device at the gate; (2) integrated with a third-party parking/ANPR system — guest enters their plate number, which is whitelisted so the barrier opens automatically on arrival. Both flows are to be supported in the app.

Agreed direction (Qossai): the specific technology/vendor is secondary to achieving an accurate per-ride count, however it's implemented (sensor, camera/CCTV, or manual); requested Allam check with an existing large-scale operator (Warner Bros. World was cited, which has a visible wait-time display) to understand what counting technology they use as a real-world reference before committing to an approach.
